tldr: The authors developed "TacPrint," a wearable fingertip tactile sensor costing only about $50 with a thickness of 7.8 mm. By reconstructing high-resolution contact-depth maps from 24 capacitive channels, it dramatically improves robot grasping and contact reproduction success rates.
hero_caption: Overall concept of TacPrint. It can be worn on both human fingertips and robot hands. From 24 sparse capacitive channels, it estimates a dense 35 × 26 contact-depth map to reproduce and utilize delicate contact states.
overview:
Learning robot skills from human demonstrations has attracted widespread attention, but conventional systems have mainly focused on capturing camera images and hand kinematics. However, for dexterous grasping and manipulation tasks, contact information—how fingertips touch objects—is indispensable. Many existing tactile sensors rely on internal cameras and are bulky, making them too cumbersome for humans to wear while demonstrating natural motions, or too expensive and difficult to deploy across robot platforms.

To solve this, the authors proposed "TacPrint," a low-cost, compact wearable fingertip tactile sensor. It adds only 7.8 mm of thickness to the fingertip and costs around $50 to fabricate. Inside, 24 capacitive cells (taxels) align one-to-one with protrusions on the inner surface of a silicone skin to accurately capture localized indentations. Furthermore, the authors built a "real-to-sim-to-real" pipeline combining physical indentation data with a physics simulator to train a model that estimates a dense 35 × 26 contact-depth map from just 24 sparse signals.

Evaluation on a physical test bench showed high estimation accuracy, with a mean contact-position error of 0.250 mm and a mean depth absolute error of 0.085 mm. In human-to-robot demonstration replay experiments, applying normal-direction fingertip compensation based on the estimated contact depth improved fruit grasping success rates from 0% to 91.67% and whiteboard wiping from 0% to 90%. In closed-loop grasping with position adjustment, dense depth feedback raised the success rate under edge-contact conditions to 85%, demonstrating strong practical benefits.
contributions: Developed "TacPrint," a low-profile (7.8 mm thick) and low-cost (~$50) wearable tactile sensor that easily mounts onto human fingers and various robot hands.
Designed a mechanical structure with hemispherical protrusions on the inner silicone surface aligned one-to-one with 24 capacitive taxels to enable localized contact transmission.

Established a learning method that links physical indentation motions with a physics simulator to auto-generate ground-truth depth labels, using an LSTM to reconstruct dense 35 × 26 contact-depth maps from sparse 24-channel signals.

Demonstrated on real hardware that accurate tactile feedback substantially improves performance in normal-direction compensation for human demonstration replay and closed-loop robot grasping adjustment.

sections.heading: Why We Need Fingertip-Wearable Tactile Sensors Now
sections.summary: Human demonstrations are crucial for robots to learn dexterous manipulation, but traditional collection methods miss contact states. To address bulky existing sensors that hinder natural human motion, the authors propose TacPrint, a low-profile, inexpensive wearable sensor.
sections.details:
High-quality demonstration data is the foundation of robot skill acquisition. Recently, human-centric data collection—where humans demonstrate tasks directly using their own hands rather than via teleoperation—has become popular. It provides a natural, intuitive way to teach complex motions.

However, most current data collection pipelines record only visual inputs from cameras and kinematic information such as hand poses and trajectories. This completely misses the fingertip contact state, which is the most critical element when grasping or pressing objects.

While optical tactile sensors with built-in cameras and high-density capacitive arrays have been developed to measure contact geometry and depth, practical barriers remain: they are often too bulky for humans to wear while demonstrating natural motions, can only fit specific robot hands, or are simply too expensive.

To overcome these issues, this study introduces "TacPrint." It adds only 7.8 mm of thickness to the fingertip and costs around $50 in parts. Hemispherical protrusions on the inner surface of the silicone skin align one-to-one with 24 capacitive cells (taxels), effectively converting localized surface deformations into distinct electrical signals.

Furthermore, the authors propose a learning pipeline that reconstructs a dense 35 × 26 contact-depth map from these 24 sparse measurements using a temporal sequence model. This captures rich contact information without hindering natural human operation, enabling reliable transfer and online compensation on robots.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Data Collection and Wearable Tactile Thimbles
sections.summary: Human-centric data collection has evolved from handheld grippers to barehanded demonstrations, but capturing contact details remained difficult. Meanwhile, existing thimble-type tactile sensors struggled to balance wearability, rich information, and low cost.
sections.details:
This study builds on two major research streams.

The first is the evolution of human-centric data collection. Early systems like UMI and FreeTacMan required operators to hold physical grippers. Later approaches such as DexCap, ARCap, and DART evolved toward tracking human fingertip motions directly with near-barehanded setups. Subsequent efforts like DexUMI and DexViTac attempted to incorporate tactile sensing, but finely capturing localized contact states remained challenging.

The second is the development of wearable fingertip tactile sensors (wearable thimbles). Devices worn on fingertips like thimbles include ThimbleSense using force/torque sensors, FingerTac using Hall-effect sensors to measure 3-axis tactile signals, and TacCap using lightweight fiber Bragg gratings (FBGs).

Although these designs demonstrated the utility of contact information, none fully met all requirements: being thin enough for natural wearing, resolving localized contact shapes, fitting diverse human finger sizes and robot fingers easily, and remaining inexpensive to fabricate. TacPrint was specifically designed to fill this gap.

sections.heading: Hardware Architecture and Learning Dense Depth from Sparse Signals
sections.summary: TacPrint combines silicone protrusions with a 24-channel capacitive sensor in a 7.8 mm thick form factor, secured via Velcro. A CNC stage and a physics simulator generate paired depth labels, allowing an LSTM network to predict dense depth maps from temporal capacitive signals.
sections.details:
### III-A Structure Design
The TacPrint hardware consists of three components: a silicone skin, a 24-channel capacitive sensing unit (SNIOW Technology), and a 3D-printed support frame.

The silicone skin uses Mold Star 20T (shore hardness 20A). Its inner surface features a 6 × 4 array of 24 hemispherical protrusions with a radius of 0.7 mm. Because each protrusion directly matches the capacitive taxel beneath it, external contact pressure transfers locally into each cell rather than spreading across neighbors.

An adjustable Velcro strap serves as the fastener. In a test with 12 human participants (finger widths 14–18 mm, circumferences 45–58 mm), TacPrint achieved high ratings: 4.76/5 for stability and 4.87/5 for comfort. Mounting onto robot hands (such as LinkerHand O20 or Tesollo grippers) is also straightforward using custom connectors and Velcro.

### III-B Tactile-to-Depth Learning Pipeline
This pipeline reconstructs a dense 35 × 26 (910 pixels) contact-depth map from 24 sparse capacitive signals through three key steps:

- **1) Tactile Data Collection**: TacPrint is mounted on a 3-axis XYZ linear stage (CNC stage). Indenters of various shapes press into the sensor at precise positions and depths, recording synchronized 24-channel capacitive data.
- **2) Simulated Depth Label Generation**: Identical indenter shapes, contact positions, and penetration depths are recreated in an Isaac Gym/Flex-based physics simulator (TacFlex). The silicone elastomer is modeled as a tetrahedral mesh. The computed surface deformation field is rasterized into a 35 × 26 depth map (normalized to a maximum of 3 mm) as ground-truth labels. On the physical stage, simulation labels matched real contacts closely, with a contact-center depth error of 0.110 mm and a position error of 0.247 mm.
- **3) Temporal Learning**: To account for capacitive hysteresis (different responses during loading vs. unloading), the model takes a 9-frame temporal window ($T=9$) including the 4 preceding and 4 succeeding frames. A single-layer unidirectional LSTM (hidden dimension 256) extracts temporal features, and a spatial decoder with transposed convolutions outputs the 35 × 26 depth map. The loss function uses a foreground-weighted scheme that penalizes errors in contact regions more heavily.

sections.heading: Depth Estimation Accuracy, Human Demo Replay, and Closed-Loop Grasping
sections.summary: Three experiments validate the system: depth estimation accuracy (0.250 mm position error), robot reproduction of human demos with contact compensation (grasping success jumped from 0% to 91.67%), and real-time closed-loop grasping adjustment (edge-contact success doubled from 45% to 85%).
sections.details:
### Objectives and Experimental Setup
This section addresses three questions:
- Q1: Can consistent contact depth and position be accurately estimated from sparse capacitive signals?
- Q2: Can tactile feedback from TacPrint improve robot reproduction of vision-based human demonstrations?
- Q3: Is the estimated dense depth map more effective than raw taxel signals in closed-loop grasp adjustment?

### Exp. 1: Contact Characterization (Estimation Accuracy)
On the test set against simulation labels, the model achieved a contact-region RMSE of 0.223 mm, a weighted-centroid error of 1.213 pixels, and an IoU of 0.829.
In 40 controlled trials on the physical CNC stage, the mean absolute error at the contact center was 0.085 mm. Across the 37 trials where contact regions were not truncated by sensor boundaries, the mean contact-position error was 0.250 mm. This confirms that millimetric and sub-millimetric contact details can be recovered from just 24 low-resolution channels.

### Exp. 2: Human-Centric Data Collection and Robot Replay
An operator wore TacPrints and AprilTags on their thumb, index, and middle fingers to demonstrate grasping fruits (apple, mango, peach) and wiping a whiteboard with an eraser. These tasks were replayed on a RealMan arm with a LinkerHand.
Direct replay of the visual tracking trajectories caused the fingers to slip off the objects without making firm contact, yielding a 0% grasping success rate. When adding tactile compensation—multiplying the average of the top 10 predicted depth values by a gain and pushing fingertips in their normal directions—fruit grasping success soared to 91.67% (95% for apple, 100% for mango, 80% for peach). Whiteboard wiping also jumped from 0% (dropping the eraser) to 90% (completing two full wiping cycles).

### Exp. 3: Contact-Aware Closed-Loop Grasping
A mock orange was placed across 8 horizontally offset positions and grasped using a Tesollo two-finger gripper. Three methods were compared: "Contact Only" (stopping on contact), "Raw Taxels" (adjusting gripper position via 24-channel centroid), and "Dense Depth" (adjusting via estimated 35 × 26 depth centroid).
Overall success rates were 37.5% for Contact Only, 67.5% for Raw Taxels, and 87.5% for Dense Depth. Under challenging edge-contact conditions (Pos. 1, 2, 7, 8), Raw Taxels dropped to 45%, whereas Dense Depth maintained 85%. The raw sparse centroid tends to bias toward the array center and trigger premature stops, whereas the dense depth map accurately captures boundaries, enabling effective recentering.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Low-Profile Tactile Sensing for Manipulation
sections.summary: TacPrint is a practical sensor combining low cost and thin profile with machine learning to extract dense contact-depth information. Future work will target better generalization to unseen objects and reconstructing finer contour details.
sections.details:
This work presented TacPrint, a wearable fingertip tactile sensor achieving a compact 7.8 mm profile at around $50. By combining mechanical design via silicone protrusions with a simulator-driven temporal learning pipeline, the authors demonstrated that dense 35 × 26 contact-depth maps can be accurately estimated from sparse 24-channel capacitive signals.

This rich tactile representation proved powerful both for contact compensation during human demonstration replay (91.67% grasping, 90% wiping success) and for closed-loop grasping adjustments on a robot (85% success on edge contacts).

The paper also discusses current limitations openly:
- Because the sensor uses a sparse array of 24 cells, completely reconstructing fine edge geometries and intricate micro-contours remains difficult.
- The geometric features of the indenters used during training may bias depth predictions.
- Physical real-world validation was limited to center depth and contact position, leaving full-field pixel-wise deformation across the elastomer surface unmeasured.

Future research will focus on improving robustness across diverse contact objects and mounting conditions, boosting prediction fidelity, and further refining wearability.

takeaways: Aligning inner silicone protrusions one-to-one with capacitive taxels isolates localized deformations and prevents signal crosstalk across cells.
Even with sparse sensor inputs (24 channels), a "real-to-sim-to-real" pipeline linking CNC indentation data with physics simulation can successfully upsample signals into dense depth maps (35 × 26).
In vision-based human demo replay, applying subtle fingertip adjustments along the contact normal based on tactile depth drastically improves manipulation success rates.
In closed-loop control, raw sparse taxel centroids bias toward the sensor center; converting signals to dense depth maps is crucial for accurate edge-contact detection and centering.
limitations: Relying on sparse 24-channel inputs limits the sensor's ability to faithfully resolve fine surface textures and intricate edge features.
Because the training pipeline relies on rigid indenter indentations, generalizing to unseen compliant objects or complex arbitrary shapes remains challenging.
Real-world physical validation evaluated only contact-center position and maximum depth consistency, without directly measuring full-field deformation fields across the entire elastomer surface.
